The Austro-Hungarian Empire. This multinational state in Central and Eastern Europe lasted from eighteen sixty-seven to nineteen eighteen, comprising the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary under a single monarch. Created by the Compromise of eighteen sixty-seven following Austria's military defeats, it was one of Europe's great powers despite its ethnic and religious diversity, managing a complex political settlement among Austrians, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Ukrainians, Romanians, Croats, Serbs, and other peoples. Its collapse at the end of World War One fragmented the region into numerous independent nation-states, fundamentally reshaping European geography and politics.

The Compromise of eighteen sixty-seven established the Dual Monarchy, granting Hungary virtual autonomy within the empire under a joint monarchy, with separate parliaments and governments for Austria and Hungary while retaining common foreign policy, defense, and finance. The empire was ruled by the Habsburg dynasty, specifically Emperor Francis Joseph the First from eighteen forty-eight to nineteen sixteen, the longest-reigning European monarch, whose sixty-eight-year reign spanned the empire's rise and final catastrophic decline. The Austro-Hungarian Empire was a patchwork of diverse ethnicities and languages including Austrians, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Ukrainians, Romanians, Croats, and Serbs, creating perennial tensions between the dominant Germans and Hungarians and the subject peoples seeking autonomy.

Vienna was the empire's capital and one of Europe's great cultural centers, the residence of emperors and birthplace of classical music composers Beethoven, Mozart, Strauss, and Brahms, and a leading intellectual hub. The empire was a Catholic multinational polity, permitting other Christian denominations and Judaism but with substantial Orthodox Christian and Muslim minority populations in its Balkan provinces. The Balkans, the empire's southeastern territory acquired via the Treaty of Berlin in eighteen seventy-eight, encompassed Bosnia-Herzegovina and other regions with Slavic and Orthodox Christian majorities, whose aspirations for independence provoked constant regional tension.

The Ausgleich, the compromise, reserved foreign policy for the common monarch and shared ministries, while Hungary retained more autonomy than other regions, creating resentment among other nationalities and making imperial governance increasingly fragile. The empire was a great power militarily and economically as its Austro-Hungarian Army was one of Europe's largest, and its industries, agriculture, and financial markets sustained the empire's status and its role in great-power politics.

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne, in Sarajevo in nineteen fourteen by a Serbian nationalist triggered the diplomatic crisis that led to World War One, in which the empire fought on the Central Powers side. The empire's military disasters in World War One, economic collapse, nationalist uprisings, and the empire's defeat in nineteen eighteen led to the Treaty of Trianon in nineteen twenty, which dismembered it into Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Romania enlarged, and Poland.
